P	A farming village on the eastern edge of the <b>Flats</b> (page 126), on a bluff overlooking the <b>Great Wood</b> (page 200). A great, rune-etched megalith stands amidst a cluster of squat stone homes, surrounded by an arc of farmland.
P	The PCs call this village home. It's a tight-knit community, poor but a good place to live. Everyone is expected to pull their weight, but few think badly of those who suffer misfortune. The town pulls together; its community is its strength.
H2	Places
HR
B	The <b>Stone</b> is well over 50 feet tall and etched in faded runes. It seems older than even the <b>Maker</b>-ruins (page 264) upon which the village was founded. When storms roll in, lightning strikes the Stone repeatedly.
B	The <b>Cistern</b> is an underground vault, clearly an artifact of the Makers. Locals fill it with rain, snow, and water from the <b>Stream</b> (page 396).
B	The <b>public house</b> is a large hall, where folks meet after sundown to drink and socialize. It offers floor space to travelers and a small stable under the same roof. The town's horses are kept here.
B	The <b>granary</b> is a warehouse built on a Maker-ruin foundation. Foodstuffs are stored here. Everyone contributes, everyone shares.
B	The <b>pavilion of the gods</b> is an openair structure with shrines to <b>Aratis</b> (page 22), <b>Danu</b> (page 64), <b>Helior</b> (page 224), <b>Tor</b> (page 452), and maybe others (page 178). As close as Stonetop gets to a temple.
PAGE	13
B	The <b>Ringwall</b> is a waist-high fence of fieldstones, 2-3 feet thick. It won't keep out serious raiders, but provides a little cover if needed. Homes beyond it are newer, built by immigrants or younger families.
B	<b>Watchtowers</b> stand along the Ringwall, a dozen feet tall or so. One to the north, one to the southeast, one to the southwest. Villagers rotate through watch duty at night.
B	A <b>switchback path</b> leads down the bluff to the <b>Stream</b> (page 396) and the <b>Great Wood</b> (page 200). Climbing it takes 10-15 minutes, longer with a heavy load.
B	The <b>fields</b> stretch out around the town, about 1,000 acres total. A third of the land sits fallow each year, with the rest growing barley, oats, beans, and potatoes. Farmers work the fields communally, rather than as familial plots.
B	The <b>Old Wall</b> wraps around the fields, about a mile from the Stone itself and at the end of the <b>West Road</b> (page 270). Clearly once a mighty rampart, it has tumbled and been buried by the ages. When the villagers need stone for construction, they dig it out of the old wall and haul it back to town.

H2	People
P	Around 300 souls live in Stonetop, or about 50 families. Everyone knows everyone else, at least by name and reputation. Most families have been here for many generations, tied together by kinship and marriage.
ICON	icons/people.svg
P	The village supports only a few full-time <b>tradesfolk</b>: a smith, a tanner, a potter, a midwife, and a publican. (5 souls, plus 5-10 assistants/apprentices)
ICON	icons/people.svg
B	<b>Hunters and trappers</b> ply the wood for meat and fur, and also forage for fruits, vegetables, mushrooms, and useable wood. Trappers produce much of the village's wealth, but hunters range farther and have more prestige. (10-20 souls)
ICON	icons/people.svg
B	<b>Farmers</b> work the fields, producing the village's staple foods. Hard, physical work. Most practice "minor" trades on the side, like carpentry, stonecutting, thatching, husbandry, distilling, etc. (~75 souls)
ICON	icons/people.svg
B	<b>Homemakers</b> keep the village running. They cook, clean, tend gardens, spin, weave, sow, mind children, practice a dozen minor trades, and otherwise manage a household. Families might have 2 or 3 homemakers each, from across generations. (~100 souls)
ICON	icons/people.svg
B	<b>Elders</b> have retired from the fields or the rigors of homemaking, but still help as they can. Many still serve the village as keepers of lore and wisdom. (~25 souls)
ICON	icons/people.svg
B	<b>Children</b> play and learn and grow. They also help with chores, tend livestock, chase birds from the fields, forage near the Stream, haul water, mind younger children, and so forth, gaining more and more responsibilities as they grow. (~100 souls)
PAGE	17
H2	Home & hearth
HR
P	Homes are low, squat, made of stone from the Old Wall. Roofs are thatched with barley straw. Each is heated by a central hearth. Most have small cellars, a standing loom, a small vegetable garden, and pens for livestock (inside and out).
P	Families pass homes down between generations. Larger families might occupy two or even three adjacent buildings. New homes are occasionally built just outside the Ringwall.
P	Homemakers grind grain with quernstones (as the village has no mill), to make flatbread, porridge, stew, ale, and whisky mash. They catch rainwater in clay vessels or draw water from the Cistern. Washing happens down at the <b>Stream</b> (page 396), but folks rarely go alone.
P	Clothes are mostly leather, fur, and handspun wool. Belts, pouches, torcs, and brooches are common. Shoes are cut from single pieces of leather, with tabs that wrap up and around the feet, laced together into a simple sandal or pump. To make "boots," folks add thick wool socks, maybe lined with fur.
P	Timber is relatively scarce. Because of the <b>Compact</b> (page 201), villagers won't fell a living tree from the Great Wood. Folks scavenge deadfall for firewood and smaller projects, and grow saplings around the fields and Old Wall for spears, bows, and arrows. Large-scale construction requires trading for timber or a logging trip to the <b>Foothills</b> (page 144).
Q	Where does ___ live?
Q	What task or chore are you working on?
Q	What's the best/worst thing about this chore?
Q	What's cooking on the hearth?
Q	What here makes the place feel like home?
Q	What about your home would you change if you could?
PAGE	18
H2	Trade & commerce
HR
P	Stonetop's economy is based on cooperation and sharing, trade and barter, gifts and favors, debts and honor. "Shops" aren't a thing and prices aren't fixed. Coins are rarely used between neighbors; that stuff's for outsiders and passing merchants. Crops from the fields go to the granary, to be rationed out to households.
P	Each family tends its own gardens (vegetables, gourds, fruits, and herbs) and livestock (chickens, goats, sheep, some pigs).
P	Folks practice trades part-time (spinning, weaving, sewing, leatherwork, thatching, carpentry, distilling whisky, stonecutting, husbandry, etc.). Neighbors swap goods and favors freely, with little worry about trades being "fair." If you need a thing that someone isn't using, they'll probably let you borrow or even take it. Maybe you help them fix their roof next month, or your husband sends over a jug of his next batch of whisky.
P	Hunters, trappers, foragers, and full-time tradesfolk tend to freely share their skills and goods, just as the farmers share their crops.
P	Still, they are often awash in gifts of gratitude from other households, and these positions all carry respect and status in town.
P	Merchants come through at least once each season (except winter). Those coming from <b>Marshedge</b> (page 274) bring textiles, rope, salt, herbs, glass, and finer goods from <b>Lygos and the South</b> (page 256). Merchants coming from <b>Gordin's</b> <b>Delve</b> (page 190) bring metals, tools, and sometimes timber. Both are keen to acquire whisky and furs. Merchants heading to Gordin's Delve are always interested in grain and livestock.
Q	What sorts of livestock does your household keep?
Q	What from your (family's) garden are you (they) most proud of?
Q	Who taught you how to ___?
Q	Who in the village is the best weaver/ carpenter/___?
Q	Who in town has a reputation as a layabout?
Q	Who tends to handle trade with outsiders?
H3	Whisky
P	Distilling whisky is a local tradition. Most households have a basic still and make a batch or two each year. Ferment some barley mash, distill it into moonshine, age it for a few weeks in a ceramic jug with toasted wood chips. Repeat. A handful of locals (like the publican, perhaps?) have larger operations with charred wooden firkins or barrels.
P	Stonetop whisky is a much-valued trade good, one of the village's chief exports. The secrets of making it are poorly understood outside the village, and even emigrants have struggled to reproduce it in other locales.
Q	Who in town makes the best whisky?
Q	According to local lore, where did the art of distilling whisky come from?
Q	Why do you think outsiders have failed to reproduce this process?
Q	What secret ingredient/step sets your (family's) whisky apart?

H2	Governance
HR
P	Stonetop has no government, just leaders.
P	Everyone knows who they are: the wise, the cunning, the brave. It's not a formal thing.
Q	When big decisions need to be made, how does the village make them? (A big meeting? A council of elders? Or what?)
Q	Who rations out crops from the granary?
Q	Whose lead do the farmers follow?
Q	To whom do the homemakers listen?
Q	Whom do the hunters/trappers respect?
Q	To whom do folks look to settle disputes/break up fights/deal with trouble?
Q	What consequences are traditional for lying/theft/assault/murder/etc.?
H2	Defense
HR
P	Able-bodied adults are expected to know how to fight and protect the village when needed. Everyone keeps a spear, a round wooden shield, and maybe a bow.
P	Folks rotate through guard duty, manning the watchtowers each night. The chief concerns are monsters from the <b>Great</b> <b>Wood</b> (page 200), especially <b>crinwin</b> (page 58), and <b>bandits</b> (page 131) or <b>Hillfolk</b> (page 228) raiding from the <b>Flats</b> (page 126). Most nights, though, the worst things you have to deal with are boredom, nerves, and bad weather.
Q	Who runs drills for the militia? Where do they typically drill?
Q	Have the watchtowers always been there, or are they a recent thing?
Q	How are watchtower shifts assigned?
Q	What's the worst part of watch duty?
Q	What's the best part?
Q	How do you keep yourself awake?
Q	How do those on watch signal trouble?
H2	Culture and lore
P	Stonetop shares a tongue with <b>Marshedge</b> (page 274), though the accents are quite distinct. Much lore is passed on verbally, through stories, songs, and poems.
P	Local decorations are reminiscent of the runes etched in the Stone itself, and of the designs found on the Maker-ruins from which the village was built.
P	<b>Tor</b> (Rain-maker, Thunderhead, Slayer-of-Beasts, page 452) is the most popular god, and associated with the Stone itself. The pavilion of the gods also holds shrines to <b>Aratis</b> (page 22), <b>Danu</b> (page 64), <b>Helior</b> (page 224), and perhaps to other local <b>gods or spirits</b> (page 178).
Q	What clothing/markings/traits are distinctive to the people of Stonetop?
Q	What game/pastime/tradition is unique to Stonetop?
Q	What's your favorite tale of Stonetop's history?
Q	What's the scariest story that the elders tell?
Q	What's the most obvious way in which the locals honor Tor?
Q	How do folks mark or celebrate a birth?
Q	How do folks mark one's coming of age?
Q	What do folks do with their dead?
Q	Do folks revere/recognize any local spirits (of house or hearth, of field or stream, of their ancestors, etc.)? How so?

H3	The Stone
P	Where did the Stone come from? Why does it draw lightning from the sky? Who carved the ancient runes upon it, and what do they mean? What other secrets does it hold? Perhaps the Stone…
E	is a shard of <b>primordial power</b> (page 298), once revered by the Makers;
E	marks <b>Tor</b>'s (page 452) own grave;
E	was carved from <b>Tor's Fist</b> (page 481) and placed here by the god himself;
E	is the petrified remains of <b>Stormcatcher</b> (page 332);
E	binds an <b>emanation</b> of the Things Below (page 436);
E	channels lightning to power an artifact deep beneath the village;
E	was brought here by the <b>Tempest</b> <b>Lords</b> (page 398) from far across land and sea;
E	is some combination of the above; or
E	something else entirely.
HR
H3	The Cistern
P	What's down there, really? What did <b>the</b> <b>Makers</b> (page 264) build it for? Perhaps…
E	it connects to a complex of chambers and tunnels;
E	some evil thing slumbers in the water;
E	it hides an arcanum, like a variant of the <b>Preserving Runes</b> (page 518) or the <b>Ward of Still Waters</b> (page 514);
E	it's just a big vault for storing water (the Makers needed to drink, too);
E	some combination of the above; or
E	something else entirely.

HR
H3	Ruins of the past
P	What was this place, in the time of the Makers? Perhaps it was…
E	a border-fort of the <b>Stone Lords</b> (page 382);
E	a trading post of the <b>Green Lords</b> (page 210), from before the <b>Fae</b> (page 94) rebelled, where they would truck with other Makers;
E	an outpost of the <b>Tempest Lords</b> (page 398), watched over by <b>Stormcatcher</b> (page 332) and her tower before it fell into ruin;
E	a free city and market, where the various Makers came to trade and learn;
E	a place of pilgrimage for the Makers, a temple to whatever gods or powers they revered;
E	some combination of the above, perhaps changing over time; or
E	something else entirely.
P	The answer should reflect and be reflected in other details. If this was a Stone Lord border-fort, then chunks of the Old Wall could be found at the base of the bluff, down in the Great Wood. If this was a Tempest Lord outpost, then stones from the Old Wall would bear carvings like those in the <b>Ruined Tower</b> (page 332).
H3	Origins
P	The village has been here for a dozen generations at least, but the true origins of its people are shrouded in mystery and conflicting folktales.
P	Whence came the people of Stonetop?
P	What led them to settle here? Perhaps they were…
E	subjects of <b>Stormcatcher</b> (page 332), who fled here when her tower fell;
E	freed servants of the <b>Stone Lords</b> (page 382) and refugees from the <b>Barrow Builders</b> (page 34);
E	migrants from east of the <b>Dread</b> <b>River</b> (page 86), distant kin to the <b>Manmarchers</b> (page 282 and page 350)
E	migrants from across the <b>Huffel Peaks</b> (page 236), who fled the boiling seas and found succor here;
E	a people out of time and space, emerging from the portal beneath the <b>Ruined Tower</b> (page 332);
E	some combination of the above; or
E	something else entirely.
